sections.title: Concept Overview
sections.content: In Level 3, questions related to confusing words are more context-based. A long sentence usually contains an incorrect word, and you must choose the correct replacement. Sometimes the given word may seem correct in meaning, but its proper denotation or usage may differ. Therefore, it is important to check context, grammar, and precise meaning.

sections.title: Contextual Vocabulary Errors
sections.content: Step 1: Read the entire sentence carefully and understand its main idea. Step 2: Identify the word that seems incorrect according to the context. Step 3: Compare the meanings of the replacement options. Step 4: Determine which word makes the meaning of the sentence most accurate. Step 5: Read the sentence again to confirm the logical flow. Example: 'The manager complimented the new software because it improved efficiency.' Here 'complimented' is incorrect; the correct word is 'complemented'.

sections.title: Word Swap / Phrase Replacement
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the meaning of the given word or phrase. Step 2: Check whether that meaning fits the context of the sentence. Step 3: Look for an option whose denotation is more precise. Step 4: Verify both grammar and meaning. Step 5: Check the overall tone and clarity of the sentence. Example: 'He was economical with the truth.' Here 'economical' is used in the sense of 'sparing' or 'not fully honest'.

sections.title: Denotation vs Connotation
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the literal meaning (denotation) of the word. Step 2: Understand its implied meaning (connotation). Step 3: Choose the word that best fits the context. Step 4: Recognize subtle differences between similar words. Example: 'Childish' and 'Childlike' carry different connotations.

sections.title: Advanced Confusing Word Pairs
sections.content: Some advanced confusing pairs include: compliment/complement, eminent/imminent, historic/historical, assure/ensure/insure, moral/morale. These words have small but important differences in meaning.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Choosing a word based only on its surface meaning. 2. Not understanding the difference between denotation and connotation. 3. Ignoring the full sentence context. 4. Selecting a replacement without checking grammar.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 3 vocabulary questions, identifying errors requires a combination of context analysis, precise meaning, and grammar. The correct replacement is the word that maintains the meaning, tone, and grammatical accuracy of the sentence.

tricks.title: Context Priority Rule
tricks.explanation: The correct word is the one that matches the meaning of the entire sentence.
tricks.example: The teacher ensured that everyone understood the lesson.

tricks.title: Denotation Check Trick
tricks.explanation: First recall the exact dictionary meaning of the word.

tricks.title: Complement vs Compliment Trick
tricks.explanation: 'Complement' means to complete or enhance something, while 'Compliment' means to praise.
tricks.example: The red tie complements his suit.

tricks.title: Assure vs Ensure Trick
tricks.explanation: 'Assure' means to give confidence to a person, while 'Ensure' means to make something certain.
tricks.example: The teacher ensured success through practice.

tricks.title: Historic vs Historical Trick
tricks.explanation: 'Historic' refers to an important event, while 'Historical' means related to history.
tricks.example: The signing of the treaty was a historic event.

tricks.title: Tone Matching Trick
tricks.explanation: Choose a word that matches the tone of the sentence (formal or informal).

tricks.title: Full Sentence Recheck
tricks.explanation: After replacing the word, read the entire sentence again to check clarity.
tricks.example: The corrected sentence should sound natural.

tricks.title: Elimination Strategy
tricks.explanation: First remove options with incorrect meanings.
tricks.example: If the word does not indicate praise, eliminate 'compliment'.
